Catalase. An antioxidant enzyme found in nearly all aerobic organisms that catalyzes the rapid decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. It is one of the fastest enzymes known, protecting cells from oxidative damage by eliminating a toxic byproduct of aerobic metabolism. Catalase catalyzes the reaction where two molecules of hydrogen peroxide become two molecules of water and one molecule of oxygen. Its substrate is hydrogen peroxide, a toxic free radical generated in cellular organelles called peroxisomes and in mitochondria. The turnover rate is approximately one million molecules per second per enzyme molecule—among the highest of any enzyme. Catalase contains an iron-containing heme group, specifically iron protoporphyrin nine, at its active site. The enzyme is located primarily in peroxisomes, which are organelles named for hydrogen peroxide production, though it also exists in mitochondria and the cytoplasm. Catalase is a tetrameric protein with four subunits that cooperatively bind and process substrate. The enzyme's function is to prevent hydrogen peroxide accumulation, which otherwise damages proteins, lipids, and DNA through hydroxyl radical formation. Aerobic respiration inevitably generates hydrogen peroxide as electrons leak from the electron transport chain. While peroxide is chemically reactive and useful as a signaling molecule at low concentrations, high levels are poisonous. Catalase evolved as the cell's primary hydrogen peroxide scavenger, enabling the metabolic advantages of aerobic life without catastrophic oxidative stress. Its extraordinary catalytic rate reflects the cell's urgent need to eliminate peroxide before it causes damage, operating near the theoretical limit of enzyme efficiency. The enzyme's presence is essentially universal in aerobic life, underscoring its critical importance.
